*** Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa: Veṇīsaṃhāra.
Stage Director: Yudhiṣṭhira, Assistant to the Stage Director.
Bhīmasena, Arjuna, and Sahadeva.
Kṛṣṇa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Duryodhana.
Karṇa, Kṛpa, Aśvatthāman,
and Saṃjaya.
Sundaraka, an attendant of Karṇa, the chamberlain of Yudhiṣṭhira,
[and] the chamberlain of Duryodhana.
The Rākṣasa (Rudhirapriya),
an attendant of the Rākṣasa Hiḍimbā and a friend of Duryodhana.
Charioteers, gatekeepers, and Draupadī.
Bhānumatī, the wife of Duryodhana;
Gāndhārī;
and Duḥśalā, the sister of Duryodhana and wife of Jayadratha.
Rākṣasī, wife of Rudhirapriya; mother of Jayadratha; attendants of Draupadī and Bhānumatī. ***************************************************************************
The Veṇīsaṃhāra. First Act.
Though forbidden by these bees, the makaranda has been plundered; the moon’s rays, as if drenched within it, have caused the buds to burst open.
May this handful of flowers scattered at the feet of Hari grant us success, which is as beautiful to behold as the assembly itself. 1.1.
Moreover,

may the conciliation of the enemy of Kaṃsa— whose feet were placed upon the impressions of Rādhikā’s own feet, and who was covered in bristling hair as he followed her with tear-stained eyes when she departed from the Rasa dance on the banks of the Kālindī, leaving him in anger over their sport— prosper you, once his beloved had looked upon him with favor.

Moreover, may Dhūrjaṭi protect you all—[he who was seen] with affection by the Goddess; with fear and agitation by the Asura women, asking "What is this?"; with compassion by the sages whose inner essence is tranquil; with a smile by Viṣṇu; with pride as they withdrew their weapons by the heroic Daityas whose agitation for their wives had been stilled; and with joy by the deities during the burning of Maya’s city. 1.3.
[At the end of the Nāndī: Stage Manager: Enough of this prolixity.
I bow to that Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, who is free from passion and not black, and who composed the nectar called the Mahābhārata, which is to be drunk by the cupped hands of those who listen.
Looking all around:
"O distinguished leaders of the assembly, we have something to request of you.
Herein, this composition of poetry is scattered like another handful of flowers."
Like honey-bees, enjoy even the slightest fragments of virtue, however sparse they may be, as if they were drops of honey. // 1.5 //
We are now prepared to present this drama titled *Veṇīsaṃhāra*, the work of the poet Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa, who bears the insignia of the king of beasts.

Therefore, I entreat you to lend your attention here, whether out of regard for the poet’s labor, out of respect for the nobility of the plot and subject matter, or out of curiosity to behold a new drama. *(Behind the scenes)*
Sir, hurry, hurry!
Indeed, at the command of the noble Vidura, these men are summoning the entire company of actors.
Let the procedures for arranging the musical instruments and other preparations be carried out without delay.

It is said that this is the time of entry for the Discus-bearer, the son of Devakī, who— followed by a host of eminent sages such as Pārāśarya, Nārada, Tumburu, and Jāmadagnya, and having himself undertaken the mission out of a desire for the welfare of the Bharata lineage— is about to set out toward the camp of the great king Duryodhana.
The Stage Manager (having heard this, with joy):
Oh, how truly blessed is this world today, favored by the Lord Viṣṇu, who possesses the power to create, sustain, and dissolve the universe!

The entire Bharata lineage and the royal assembly were brought together by the enemy of Kaṃsa himself, acting as a messenger and the agent of peace— who was the cause for extinguishing the fire of the world-ending dissolution at the battle between these two princes of the Kuru and Pāṇḍava lines.
So why, O stage-manager, do you not begin the musical performance with the actors?
[Entering] the Stage Manager:
Very well; I shall begin.
"Based on what occasion should it be sung?
Sūtradhāra:

"Indeed, let it be based on this very [occasion]: when the circle of the quarters of the sky is whitened by the dust of the flowers of the moon, the sun, the stars, the *krauñca* and *haṃsa* flocks, the *saptacchada*, the night-lily, the white lotus, and the *kāśa* grass."
Let a musical concert be commenced, taking recourse in this autumn season whose waters and reservoirs are sweet;
for in this autumn,
the birds possess beautiful wings, possess sweet voices, have adorned the quarters of the sky, and are bold in their undertakings due to intoxication.
The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra fall upon the surface of the earth, driven by the power of time.
The Attendant (Pāripārśvika):
[With agitation] Noble sir, may there be peace!
May evil be stilled and misfortune averted!
Director: (With an embarrassed smile) My worthy friend, it is out of a desire to describe the excellence of the autumn season that swans are designated as "Dhārtarāṣṭras."
"So has the evil been stilled and the inauspiciousness averted?
The Attendant:
"Indeed, I know it well."
"Why do you suspect inauspiciousness in these words of yours? Truly, my heart seems to tremble.
Sūtradhāra:

"Worthy sir, indeed all inauspiciousness has now been warded off by the Enemy of Kaṃsa himself, who, having personally undertaken the role of a messenger, acts as a negotiator for peace. For it is thus:"
May the sons of Pāṇḍu, having extinguished the fire of enmity toward Nirvāṇa through their pacification of enemies, rejoice together with Mādhava;
and may the sons of the Kuru king, their bodies healed of wounds and their lands adorned with blood, remain in good health along with their servants.
[Offstage, with reproach: Ah, you evil-minded wretch, you base actor who recites empty benedictions!
Having struck at our lives and our accumulated wealth by means of the lacquer house, poisoned food, and entry into the assembly hall—
While I am alive, how can the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra remain at ease, they who have dragged away the garments and hair of the Pāṇḍava women? 1.8.
[Sandhyaṅga:
Upakṣepa; V 6.69] The *sūtradhāra* and the *pāripārśvika* listen.
Pāripārśvika:
Master, from where does this come? Sūtradhāra:

(Looking behind) Ah! Here indeed is Bhīmasena, enraged and followed by Sahadeva, approaching this very way from the direction of Vāsudeva. Unable to endure the alliance of the Kurus, his terrifying frown—shaped like the trident-arch of Death fixed upon the broad slope of his forehead—seems to drink us all in with a single glance.
"Therefore, it is not proper for us to remain before him. Let us go elsewhere from here.
Thus they both departed.
Prologue.
Then enters Bhīmasena, followed by Sahadeva, in a state of anger.
Bhīmasena:
"Āḥ! You evil-souled, wretched actor, you who recite false propitiatory verses!
[He] recites again, beginning with 'The lac-house'...
Sahadeva:
*With conciliation:* Noble sir, forgive us, forgive us!
This speech of this son of Bharata is indeed approved by us.
"Those who have extinguished the fire of enmity toward Nirvana speak according to the truth.
Bhīmasena says: 'May the Kurus, together with their servants, having adorned the earth with a network of blood and with mangled bodies, dwell in heaven.'"
With reproach: "Indeed, indeed, you ought not to contemplate inauspicious things regarding the Kauravas;
those brothers of yours are worthy of being reconciled with."
Sahadeva:
(With anger) Noble brother, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra have created enmity at every step.
If the king were not the restrainer, who among your younger brothers would be able to endure [this]?
Bhīmasena: So it is. For this very reason, from this day forward, I am severed from you. Behold:
that enmity which has grown in me since I was but a child toward the Kurus has no noble cause therein, neither in Arjuna nor in you two.
Just as Jarāsandha’s chest was once joined and has now grown apart again through wrath, Bhīma is breaking that alliance; you must join it back together! 1.10.
Sahadeva: [A member of the dramatic juncture; the *parikara* (elaboration) according to V, from pl2] &sahadevaḥ&:
*With conciliation:* "Noble sir, our preceptor is perhaps weary of you all, who have thus accumulated such great anger. Bhīmasena:
How could the Guru not feel weariness?
Even a Guru knows weariness; behold:
having seen the daughter of Pañcāla in such a state in the assembly of kings, and having dwelt for a long time in the forest with hunters, wearing garments of bark—
While I remain in the residence of Virāṭa, concealing my true nature through unworthy undertakings, my elder brother still feels grief for me, though not yet for the Kurus.
Therefore, Sahadeva, turn back;
and report this to the King from the words of Bhīma, who is inflamed by an indignation that has grown exceedingly great over such a long time.
Sahadeva: [reports].
"Noble one, what is it?
Bhīmasena replied:
"Inform him thus."
Immersed indeed in the sin of transgressing your command, I have remained so; I have surely incurred the reproach of those who stand among their peers, even of my younger brothers.
But for me, as I sever the Kauravas with a mace reddened by blood spurting from my wrath, for this one day you are no longer my elder, nor am I subject to your will.
(Thus he walks about haughtily.
Sahadeva: (Following him, to himself:)
"Ah! How is it that the noble one has entered the four-winged palace of the princess of Pañcāla?
Very well, I shall remain right here.
Thus he stood.
Bhīmasena:
(Turning back and looking) Sahadeva, you go; follow your teacher.
"I too shall enter the armory and become your companion with weapons.
Sahadeva said:
"Noble brother, this is not an armory; this is the four-winged palace of the Princess of Pañcāla."
Bhīmasena: (Reflecting) What indeed is this? Is this armory not rather the four-winged palace of the Princess of Pañcāla?
*Smiling slightly with joy:* "I must address Pāñcālī;
*affectionately taking Sahadeva by the hand*..."
"My child, please come.
Since the noble one is afflicting us while desiring peace with the Kurus, you too should observe this.
*Both act out entering.*
Sahadeva:
Noble brother, here is a seat spread out;
let the noble one sit here and await the arrival of Kṛṣṇā.
Bhīmasena: (Sitting down) My dear child, by this introduction regarding Kṛṣṇā’s arrival, it has been brought to my mind.
Then Sahadeva said: "Noble brother, for what price was the Blessed Kṛṣṇa sent to Suyodhana to make peace? For five villages."
Bhīmasena:
[Covering his ears] Alas, woe! That even the majesty of His Majesty Ajātaśatru has been diminished to such an extent—truly, my heart seems to tremble.
"O dear child, having turned back and stood there, you did not speak and I did not hear;
for such was the formidable and most fierce kṣatriya splendor of this king."
While he was playing with dice at that time, surely even that was lost by him.
*(Behind the scenes)* Compose yourself, compose yourself,
my lady! Compose yourself, compose yourself!
Sahadeva:
(Looking toward the tiring-room;
to himself) Ah! Why is Yājñasenī approaching the noble one with her eyes veiled by a steadily gathering mass of tears?
A most grievous calamity has now befallen us:
for today, as the Noble One is enraged, a light like that of lightning has been gathered; surely this dark cloud will increase it, just as the rainy season increases the storm.
Then enters Draupadī and a maidservant as previously described.
Draupadī sighs with tears.
Maidservant:
"Take heart, take heart,
my lady! Prince Bhīmasena, whose anger is as constant as the kuruvinda gem,
will remove your resentment."
"The prince Bhīmasena, whose enmity toward the Kurus is ever-persistent, will take away your anger.
Draupadī:
Friend Buddhimatī, this may be so if he becomes an adversary to the Great King.
SktCh_3: "O clever girl, what will happen if this becomes unfavorable to the Great King?
Maid:
"The prince is standing right here."
Therefore, let the lady approach him;
here the prince stands,
so let the lady draw near to him.
Draupadī: Girl, let us do so. SktCh_5: Girl, let us do so.
*As they walk about:* Maid:
Victory, victory to the Prince!
"Victory! Victory to the Prince!
Bhīmasena, not hearing what that formidable voice had said, recites it again.
Maid:
My lady, the prince appears as if he is quite agitated.
Draupadī:
Girl, if it is so, then even this contempt inspires confidence in me.
Therefore, sitting here, I shall first hear what my lord intends to do.
"Girl, if that is so, then even this slight disregard of mine provides me with comfort.
Therefore, sit here and listen for a moment to what my lord has resolved. Both do as they are told.
Bhīmasena (with anger, addressing Sahadeva):
What, indeed, is this peace for the sake of five villages?
I shall not crush the hundred Kauravas in battle out of anger, nor shall I drink the blood from Duḥśāsana’s chest;
I shall not smash Suyodhana’s thighs with my mace—let the king make peace with you on these terms.
Draupadī:
(With joy,
aside) My lord, such words as these have indeed never been heard from you before!
Therefore, please speak once more:
"O Lord, such words as these have indeed never been heard before;
pray, speak them again."
Bhīmasena:
(Without even listening) He recites again, "I shall churn," and so forth.
Sahadeva:
"Noble sir, has the Great King's message been received as if it were incomprehensible?
Bhīmasena replied,
"And what, pray, would be its comprehension in this case?"
Sahadeva:
Noble brother, this is exactly what the Guru has commanded.
Bhimasena: [Agrees.]
"To whom? "To Sahadeva.
"To Suyodhana."
Bhīmasena: What is it?
Sahadeva:
"Grant us the four villages of Indraprastha, Vṛkaprastha, Jayanta, and Vāraṇāvata, and let there be some fifth one as well. (1.16)
Bhīmasena: What happened after that?
Sahadeva:

Thus, by this request for each name and village, and because the fifth [name] is not mentioned, I believe this is merely an exposure of the sites of injury, such as the eating of poison, the burning of the house of lac, and the gambling hall. Bhīmasena: (With arrogance)
Child, what is accomplished by doing this?
Sahadeva:
Noble brother, by doing this, one reveals to the world a heart that fears the extinction of its own lineage, and the incurability of the Kuru king is demonstrated.
Bhīmasena:
All of this is likewise useless.
The fact that the Kuru king is not to be made peace with was pointed out at that very time when we all, departing from here for the forest, vowed the destruction of the entire Kuru lineage.
Moreover, in this world, does the destruction of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s lineage cause you shame?
Furthermore, O fool,
does the destruction of an enemy's family in this world bring shame upon you because of your anger?
He feels no shame at having his hair pulled in the assembly by his wives.
Draupadī:
My lord, these people feel no shame;
you too must not forget this.
"O Lord, these men are not ashamed;
you, too, must not forget.
Bhīmasena said:
[With remembrance] My child, why does Pāñcālī delay?
Sahadeva:
"Noble sir, what indeed was the time when her ladyship arrived? Yet, because she was under the sway of a fit of rage, she was not noticed by you even though she had come.
Bhīmasena:
"O Queen, having seen you with such reverence, we were so overcome by our rising indignation that even though you had arrived, we did not perceive you;
therefore, you ought not to feel resentment."
Draupadī: My lord,
anger is directed toward you when you are indifferent,
but not when you are angry.
Bhīmasena:
If this is so, then consider yourself free from humiliation.
(Taking him by the hand, seating him at his side, and looking at his face.)
But why do I perceive you as if troubled?
Draupadī:
My lord, what cause for distress could there be while you are present?
SktCh_12: "O Lord, what is the cause of this agitation while you are present here?
Bhīmasena said:
"Why do you not tell me?"
*Having observed her hair:* Or rather, what is the use of reporting this while the sons of Pāṇḍu are still alive and have not gone far away?
That the daughter of the Pāñcāla king should endure such a state!
Draupadī:
Girl Buddhimatī, inform my lord at once:
who else but me would be distressed by this humiliation?
"O clever maid, inform the Lord at once:
who else is distressed by my humiliation?
The maidservant replied:
"As the Queen commands.
[Approaching Bhīma and joining his palms in reverence:
"O Prince, even more than this, today there was a cause for the Queen's grief."
"As the Queen commands.
"Prince, even more than this was the cause of the Queen's anger today.
Bhīmasena:
What indeed could be even greater than this?
Tell me, tell me!
Who is this that acts like a moth in this forest-fire of the Kauravya lineage?
He touched her loosened braid, which was like the dark crest of a column of smoke.
Maid:
Let the prince listen.
Today, indeed, the Queen, accompanied by Ambā and surrounded by her circle of sisters-in-law headed by Subhadrā, went to pay homage at the feet of the noble Gandhālī.
SktCh_15: Let the prince listen.
Today, indeed, the Queen Ambā, accompanied by the group of co-wives headed by Subhadrā and surrounded by them, went to pay homage at the feet of the noble Gāndhārī.
Bhīmasena:
This is appropriate;
indeed, the gurus are worthy of veneration.
And what follows from that?
Maid:
Then, as she was returning, she was seen by Bhānumatī.
Bhīmasena:
(With anger) Ah! She has been seen by the wife of the enemy!
Ah, this is the place of the Goddess’s anger! And what of it? Maid:
Then, having looked at the queen while casting her gaze toward the face of her friend, she said with pride and a slight smile:
Bhīmasena:
Not only was it seen, but it was also spoken of!
Oh, what shall we do? And then what happened next?
Maid:
Yajñasenī, it is heard that five villages are being requested;
why then are your hair-locks not yet bound?
"O Yājñasenī, it is heard that five villages were requested [in marriage];
why then are your hair not bound up even now?
Bhīmasena said:
Sahadeva, it has been heard.
Sahadeva:
What is being said here?
For she is indeed the wife of Duryodhana; look!
For through association with women, the hearts of others become like those of their husbands.
Even a sweet creeper causes fainting if it clings to a poisonous tree. 1.20.
Bhīmasena:
Intelligent lady, what was said by the Queen then? Maid:
"O Prince, if she were to be deprived of her attendants, then the Queen would say so. Bhīmasena: [repeats].
"What, then, have you said? Maid:
"I myself have said this."
"O Bhānumatī, while your hair remains unbound, how can our queen’s hair be tied?"—
thus was it said by me.
"O Bhānumatī, as long as your hair is not released, how can the hair of our queen be bound?"
Bhīmasena:
(With satisfaction) Well done, wise lady! Well done!
"That which was spoken—
namely, that she gives her own ornaments to Buddhimatikā, which are suitable for our attendants—
hear this, O noble daughter of the King of Pañcāla."

And in no long time, O Queen, Bhīma shall dishevel your hair with hands smeared red with thick, congealed blood from the thighs of Suyodhana, whose pair of legs have been crushed by the blows of his fierce mace whirled by his trembling arms.
[Interlude / Insertion: *parinyāsa* (V 6.71) from pl3] &Draupadī&:
"O Lord, what is difficult for you when you are so provoked? Let your brother favor this resolve of yours."
May your brothers favor this resolve of yours.
(This is the *vilobhana* [enticement], a sub-component of the *saṃdhi*.)
Sahadeva: We have been favored by this.
(A great clamor behind the scenes.)
Everyone listens with astonishment.
Bhīmasena:

Deep as the roar of Mount Mandara as it tumbles, submerged in the ocean waters churned by the churning-stick, and fierce from the mutual clashing of thundering clouds at the dissolution of the world when struck by the drumstick—[this is the sound].

Who is striking this drum—the foremost messenger of Kṛṣṇa’s wrath, a wind of calamitous thunder that brings about the destruction of the Kuru clan, and a friend to the echoing resonance of our own lion-roars? (1.22)
Entering in great agitation,
the Chamberlain says: "Prince, this indeed is the Blessed One, Vāsudeva."
All rise with palms joined in reverence;
Bhīmasena [rises] with agitation.
"Where is that Blessed One?
The Chamberlain replied: "He has begun to subdue Suyodhana, who was provoked by his partiality for the Pāṇḍavas."
*All act out agitation.* Bhīmasena:
Is he bound?
Chamberlain: No, indeed not; he has begun to restrain himself.
Bhīmasena: [continues]
"What was done by the King?

Chamberlain: "Then that Great-souled One, having cast aside the Kuru clan who had been rendered unconscious by the onset of the splendor of his manifested universal form (*viśvarūpa*), arrived at our camp."
Bhīmasena desires to see Kāmāra without delay;
[he speaks] with derision.

"What, does that evil-minded Suyodhana wish to restrain the Blessed One? [Looking into the sky] "Ah, you evil-minded defiler of the Kuru lineage! Since you have thus transgressed the bounds of propriety, the wrath of the Pāṇḍavas must manifest through you as its mere instrument."
Sahadeva:
Noble brother, does that evil-minded Suyodhana not even recognize the Blessed Vāsudeva in his true form?
Bhīmasena: [He does not.]
Child, this wicked soul is indeed deluded;
how could he know? Behold:

those who delight in the Self, whose minds are fixed on the non-conceptual samādhi, whose knots of darkness are shattered by the abundance of knowledge, and who are established in pure being— [they alone can know].
How can this one, blinded by delusion, know that ancient God whom even those who behold Him as something beyond both darkness and light do not perceive?
Noble Jayandhara, what does the Guru intend now?
Chamberlain: The Prince will go there himself and learn the Maharaja’s decision.
[Thus he exits.
[After a tumultuous noise behind the scenes:
O you commanders of our akṣauhiṇīs—Drupada, Virāṭa, the Vṛṣṇis, the Andhakas, Sahadeva, and the rest—and you foremost warriors of the Kaurava army, listen, sirs!

That fire of Yudhiṣṭhira’s wrath, which was once suppressed with effort by his mind fearing the breach of truth and vows, and which the tranquil one desired to forget out of a wish for his family's peace— that great flame now expands within the forest of the Kurus, fanned by the gambling match and kindled by the dragging of the king’s wife’s hair and garments.
Bhīmasena:
(Having heard this;
with joy) Let the light of my noble brother’s wrath, its course unimpeded, yawn and expand!
Draupadī:
My lord, why is this drum of battle being struck moment by moment,
sounding as deep as the thundering of clouds at the time of universal dissolution?
Bhīmasena:
O Queen, what else? The sacrifice is proceeding.
Draupadī:
What is this sacrifice? SktCh_23: What is this sacrifice?
Bhīmasena:
It is a sacrifice of battle. For thus it is:

we four are the officiating priests; the blessed Hari is the instructor of the ritual; the king, consecrated for the sacrifice of war, is the patron; and his queen, who has undertaken her vow, is the wife.

The Kauravas are the sacrificial animals; the appeasement of the suffering caused by the humiliation of his beloved is the fruit; and the drum of his abundant fame resounds loudly for the invitation of the kings. 1.25.
Sahadeva:
Noble brother, now that we have received permission from our elders, let us go to perform what is appropriate for our lineage.
Bhīmasena:
Child, we are indeed ready to carry out the noble one’s command.
Rising,
O Queen, let us now depart for the destruction of the Kuru lineage.
Draupadī: (Holding back her tears) My lord,
may there be auspiciousness for you, just as there was for Hari when he was about to face the battle against the Asuras.
"O Lord, may there be auspiciousness for you, like that of Hari when facing battle with the Asuras.
Both:
"The words of auspiciousness have been accepted by us."
Draupadī:
And furthermore, my lord, you must return from the battlefield once more and comfort me.
Bhīmasena:
O daughter of the King of Pañcāla, why still this false consolation?
[Her] face is once more distressed by humiliation, exhaustion, and shame.
Do you not see Vṛkodara, who has left no Kaurava remaining?
Draupadī:
My lord, do not, do not! Do not wander about disregarding your own body, with the fire of anger kindled by the insult to Yajñasenī.
For it is heard that the enemy forces must be traversed with great vigilance.

"O Lord, do not, indeed, do not! Do not wander about regardless of your bodies with the fire of your wrath ignited by the insult to Yājñasenī; for it is heard that the enemy forces must be approached with vigilance. Bhīmasena said:

O noble Kṣatriya lady, the sons of Pāṇḍu are experts at moving about within the waters of the singular ocean of battle—a place where the mud consists of the blood, fat, flesh, and brains of elephants shattered by mutual blows; where foot-soldiers stride with valor upon chariots submerged therein; and where headless trunks dance to the auspicious yet terrible sound of musical instruments, delighting in the feast of drinking copious amounts of blood.
*Thus they all exit.* End of the first act.
The second act begins.
*Then enters the Chamberlain.* Chamberlain:
I have been commanded by the great king Duryodhana.
"O upholder of the Vinaya, go quickly!
Let Queen Bhānumatī be sought out;
see whether she has returned from the time she went to pay homage at her mother's feet or not."

Since our army commanders, headed by Rādheya and Jayadratha, having seen her and being spurred on by their desire to avenge Abhimanyu, have gone to the field of battle to offer their congratulations [to Arjuna],
I must therefore depart with the utmost speed.
Oh, what sovereign power the Great King possesses, that for me, overcome as I am by old age, my only duty is to maintain the boundary of the harem!

Or rather, why should I reproach old age? For this is merely the conventional dress and behavior of all women in the inner apartments. Thus: though my eyes were capable, I did not look; though I heard, I did not listen; though I was able, I did not exercise authority, but instead took up a staff as my official insignia. With a mind intent on avoiding every stumble, I walked without arrogance. What indeed has old age done to me, whose life has been surrendered to service? (2.1)
(Walking about and looking into the air) Vihaṅgikā, Bhānumatī has returned after performing her salutations at the feet of her mother-in-law. (Listening)
"What do you say?

This Queen Bhānumatī, having performed the prostrations at the feet of the venerable deity and undertaken religious observances out of hope for her husband’s victory in battle, remains in the inner garden.
Therefore, my good lady, go about your own business while I inform the Great King that the Queen is staying here."

(Walking about) "Excellent, O devoted wife! Excellent! "It seems this was his intention: 'Just as Aśvatthāman was to be consecrated by me in the sovereignty of the earth, since he is no longer alive, the taking up of weapons by me—an old brahmin—would be in vain. It was for this reason that he acted accordingly."
Duryodhana:
(With a shake of his head) It is even so.
Karṇa:

For this very reason, that king, anticipating the mutual destruction of the royal host engaged in a great battle through partiality for the Kaurava and Pāṇḍava sides, neglected the slaughter of the principal men.
Duryodhana:
This is indeed appropriate.
Furthermore, O King, even Drupada, who has known his intentions since childhood, did not grant him residence within his own kingdom.
Duryodhana: Excellent, O King of Aṅga, excellent!
You have spoken with great skill.
Karṇa: This is not my opinion alone;
other learned men as well do not consider this to be otherwise.
Duryodhana:
So it is; what doubt can there be?
Having granted him protection, that great car-warrior was being slain by Kirīṭin.
One should disregard the King of Sindhu; otherwise, how could it be different? (3.28)
Kṛpa: (Looking) My dear child, here is Duryodhana sitting with the Sūtaputra in the shade of this banyan tree.
Therefore, let us approach him;
having done so,
both of them—
May the Lord of the Kauravas, Duryodhana, be victorious! (Having seen...)
Ah! How is it that Kṛpa and Aśvatthāman are here?
Descending from his seat, he said to Kṛpa:
"O Teacher, I salute you."
Addressing Aśvatthāman:
"Come, son of the preceptor!
Your father has been slain for our sake; embrace me with these limbs of yours, which are weary from constant toil."
This touch of your arms is like that of your father; for even in grief, it brings no change to the hairs upon your body.
Embracing him, he seats him at his side.
Aśvatthāman sheds tears.
Karṇa: [speaks].
O son of Droṇa, enough of casting yourself excessively into this fire of grief!
Duryodhana said:
O son of the preceptor, what difference is there between us two in this great ocean of calamity? Behold!
Your father was affectionate toward you and was my father’s friend; as he was a teacher to you in the science of weapons, so too was he mine.
What need is there for me to describe the grief at his passing? You yourself should know it through a mind that shares the sorrow for your teacher.
Kṛpa:
Child, it is exactly as the Lord of the Kurus has said. Aśvatthāman: [He continues:]

O King, since you are thus partial, it is indeed fitting that you should lighten the burden of your grief. But while I was alive, my father suffered the seizing of his hair; how then will other men who have sons desire to have them? (3.31)
Karṇa:
O son of Droṇa, what can be done here, now that he has brought himself to such a state by laying down his weapons—the very act which was the sole cause for protection from all humiliation?
Aśvatthāman:
O King of Aṅga, what do you say? What is to be done here?
Listen to what is being done:

Whosoever among the Pāṇḍava hosts bears a weapon with pride heavy upon his own arms; whosoever belongs to the lineage of the Pañcālas—whether a child, one of advanced age, or even one still within the womb; [all these shall be slain].
Whoever acts as a witness to that deed of mine in battle, and whoever stands in opposition—blinded by anger—I myself shall be the end-maker even of him, though he be the end-maker of the worlds.
Moreover, O Karna, disciple of Jamadagni’s son:
this is that very land where lakes were filled with the blood-water of enemies; such was the humiliation of my father—the seizing of his hair—caused by the Kshatriyas alone.
Those same brilliant weapons, heavy with the devouring of the arms of the foe, are mine. What Rama did, the wrathful son of Drona does the very same.
Duryodhana:
O son of the preceptor, what else could be more worthy of such extraordinary heroism as that, which is shared by no other?
Kṛpa:
"O King, a truly immense burden of battle has indeed been undertaken by the son of Droṇa.
Therefore, I think thus:
equipped as he is by you, he is capable of destroying even the three worlds, let alone the army of Yudhiṣṭhira."
"Therefore, let him be consecrated as commander-in-chief.
Duryodhana said:
"What you have said is most appropriate."
However, this matter was already agreed upon by the King of Aṅga.
Kṛpa said:
"O King, it is not right to neglect him as he sinks into an ocean of grief caused by an undeserved humiliation, for the sake of the King of Aṅga."
His enemy clan is also the very same one that must be disciplined;
therefore, how could he not suffer?
Aśvatthāman:
O King, Lord of the Kauravas, why even now this deliberation on what is proper and improper?

You have been awakened with great effort by these hymns of praise. Today you shall lie down for the night, having made the world devoid of Keśava, devoid of the Pāṇḍavas, and today devoid of the Somakas.
Today this narrative of war is brought to an end by the one who wields his arms; today let the exceedingly heavy burden of the earth, which has long been a forest for kings, depart.
Karṇa: (Laughing) This is easy to say, but difficult to carry out.
Many in the Kaurava army are capable of this deed.
Aśvatthāman:
O King of Aṅga, it is even so.
There are many capable men here in the Kaurava army;
however, I speak thus because I am overcome by suffering and under the sway of a fit of grief, and not out of any intent to insult heroic men.
Karṇa:

O fool, it is fitting for one who is suffering to shed tears, and for one who is enraged to enter the field of battle with his weapon as his only companion; such lamentations as these are not appropriate.
*Aśvatthāman* (speaks) with anger:
O you who have become the very burden of Rādhā’s womb, you wretched son, do you not even suggest with tears a remedy for my sorrowful self, Aśvatthāman, rather than with a weapon? Look!

My weapon has become powerless due to the words of my preceptor’s curse; like you, I have now fled from the battle out of fear. Why were you born as one who knows how to proclaim his own lineage in praise, while I was born in a family of charioteers? Why is it that I cannot counter the unpleasantness caused by this petty enemy with a weapon, but only with a missile? (3.35)
Karṇa: (With anger) O you talkative, vainly arrogant youth who has taken up weapons in vain!
"Whether lacking in vigor or possessing it, I have never cast down my weapon, as did your father, though he was mighty-armed and terrified by the Pāñcālas. (3.36)
Moreover,
whether I am a charioteer or the son of a charioteer, or whoever else I may be—
birth into a family depends on destiny, but personal prowess depends on oneself.
*Aśvatthāman:* (With anger) Ah you!
You stain upon the lineage of chariot-makers, you who are merely a burden to Rādhā’s womb! You, ignorant of weapons, do you even revile my father? Or rather—
Whether he was a coward or a hero, his strength of arm was renowned throughout the three worlds; for what he achieved in battle, this earth knows it day by day.
As for how he could have abandoned his weapons—being one who upheld the vow of truth—you, O you who are afraid of battle, are the witness; where were you then?
Karṇa: (Laughing) Thus am I a coward.
Furthermore, recollecting your father, whose sole essence was valor, a great doubt has arisen within me.
Moreover, O fool,
if they have laid down their weapons, why do those who are unarmed not ward off the enemies who still hold their arms?
That he remained indifferent even when his crown was being struck down, as if he were a woman for a very long time in the presence of the circle of kings. (3.39)
Aśvatthāman:
(With anger and trembling) O evil-souled favorite of the king, you insolent wretch of a Sūta, you who prattle incoherently!
For some reason, neither by my father—who was grieving nor fearful—nor by the hand of Drupada’s son was this [act] forbidden today;
yet, as you puff yourself up with pride in the strength of your arms, this left foot of mine is now placed upon your head. Ward him off!
Saying this, he rose to do so;
then Kṛpa and Duryodhana said:
"O son of the preceptor, forgive us!"
Thus forbidding him,
Aśvatthāman mimes the striking of a foot;
Karṇa:
*Rising up in anger and drawing his sword:* "O evil-souled one! Talkative wretch of a Brahmin! Self-praiser! Though you may well be unslayable by birth, this foot of yours shall now be uplifted!"
With this sword, you shall see it cut down and fall upon the earth.
Aśvatthāman:
O fool, what indeed is the use of this birth? Granted, I am unslayable; yet this very birth has been renounced by me.
Thus he cuts his sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).
And again, with anger:
"Today, that Kirīṭin shall be made by me one whose vow is rendered false."
Either take up a weapon, or cast it aside and place your joined palms upon your head.
Both having drawn their swords, they were intent on striking one another;
Kṛpa and Duryodhana restrained them.
Duryodhana said:
"Friend, son of the preceptor, enough with taking up arms!
Kṛpa:
"Child, son of the charioteer, enough with taking up arms!"
Aśvatthāman: Uncle, uncle, why do you restrain him?
This base son of a charioteer, bold in his insults toward my father, is likewise a partisan of Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Karṇa: O King, I must certainly not be restrained.
For those who are dull-witted and indifferent are disregarded by those of firm resolve.
This boastful talk arises from those who, though unafraid, are blinded by anger. (3.43)
Aśvatthāman:
O King, release him, release him!
Let him meet his end, easily brought about by the crushing pressure between my arms.
Moreover, O King:
whether it be out of affection or for some purpose, that you wish to protect this wicked soul who insults my father from me—that both [motives] are entirely in vain. Behold:
how can one who delights in sin be the companion of a virtuous man? How can one born of a charioteer’s lineage be the companion of one born of the Lunar dynasty?
"O King, release the diadem-wearing Arjuna! I shall today, out of wrath, make this son of Pṛthā earless before the world. (3.44)
Thus, wishing to strike,
Karṇa raised his sword.
"O talkative, lowest of brahmins, you shall not remain [alive].
O King, release him! Release him! Indeed, I am not to be restrained."
He desires to kill;
Duryodhana and Kṛpa restrain him.
Duryodhana:
Karna: O son of the preceptor, what is this delusion of yours today?
Kripa:
Child, one thing was introduced and there is agitation over something else; what is this delusion?
And at this time, it is a perverse path that this calamity of our own army should come upon this royal house from you alone.
Aśvatthāman:
Uncle, the pride of this bitter-tongued defiler of the chariot-makers' clan cannot be broken.
Kṛpa:
Child, this is truly not the time for a conflict based primarily on one's own strength.
Aśvatthāman: [Objection]...
"Uncle, if it be so,
then until this wicked man meets his end by the arrows of my enemy, I shall not abandon even my beloved weapon on the field of battle.
While this lord of armies stands here, let the King know that his dear friend’s forces are present in the fray, even though fear of the enraged Bhīma and Arjuna has arisen."
Thus he casts aside his sword.
Karṇa: (Laughing)
"For those such as you, this so-called abandonment of weapons is indeed handed down through family tradition.
Aśvatthāman:
"But, you fool! Even though weapons have not been abandoned by those like you, they are effectively abandoned long ago because they have become useless."
Karṇa: O fool!
While I am here with my weapon raised, what use are weapons for others?
Or rather, that which has not been mastered by me through the Astra-weapon—by what means shall it be mastered?

*(Behind the scenes)* Ah, you evil-minded one, you great sinner who dragged Draupadī’s hair and garments, you lowest of the Dhārtarāṣṭras! After such a long time, you have finally come before my eyes. You wretched beast, where can you go now?
Moreover, O Radheya, Duryodhana, Saubala, and others—enemies of the Pāṇḍavas, who hold bows in hand and for whom honor is the sole wealth—listen, sirs!

That dog of a king by whose hair the daughter of the King of Pañcāla was touched, by whom her garment was snatched away in the presence of kings and elders, and by whose chest-blood I have vowed to drink as wine—that very Kaurava has now fallen into the cage of my arms; let him be protected!
*All listen.* Aśvatthāman: *(With a sneer)*
O King of Aṅga, O General, O disciple of Jamadagni’s son, O you who mocked Droṇa, O you by whom the entire world is protected by the strength of your arms—
having read [the name] "Dhṛtāyudha," this very thing has now come to pass most proximately.
"Protect Duḥśāsana from Bhīma right now!
Karṇa:
"Ah! What power does Vṛkodara have to even approach the shadow of Duḥśāsana while I am alive?"
"O Prince, do not fear, do not fear!
Here I am, I have come.
Having said this, he departed.
Aśvatthāman:
O King, Lord of the Kauravas, Bhīma and Arjuna are currently churning the Kaurava army in the absence of Bhīṣma and Droṇa; they cannot be restrained by the son of Rādhā or by anyone else.
Therefore, you yourself must be intent upon countering your brother.
Duryodhana:
Ah! While I am alive and bearing arms in my hand, does that wicked soul—the son of the Wind—or anyone else, have the power even to step into the shadow of my child?
Child, do not fear, do not fear!
"Who is there? Who is here? Ho! Bring the chariot!
Having said this, he went out.
*A tumultuous noise behind the scenes.* *Aśvatthāman:* (Looking ahead)
Uncle, alas! Woe is me!
Indeed, this Kirīṭin, fearing the breach of his brother’s vow, is charging with irresistible showers of arrows against both Duryodhana and the son of Rādhā.
In every way, the blood of Duḥśāsana has been drunk by Bhīma!
Indeed, I cannot bear to behold this calamity of Duryodhana’s younger brother; for to consent to such an act is surely to sanction falsehood. Uncle, weapon against weapon!
"Untruth is better even than truth; fie on heaven! Let there be hell for me!
It is better that my weapon was abandoned—though not truly abandoned—to save Duḥśāsana from Bhīma. (3.48)
[Thinking thus, he desires to seize the sword.
(Offstage: O high-souled son of Bharadvāja, you ought not indeed to transgress a word of truth that has never before been transgressed.

Kṛpa: Child, an incorporeal voice protects you from falsehood. Aśvatthāman: [He hears it. Ah! It is the voice of my preceptor! (He falls at his feet. Preceptor, protect me! Protect me! What is this? Is it a dream? Or is it a delusion? Or has my mind, reeling from the shock of grief, become deranged? For I do not perceive that which is real, nor do I see what is unreal. Yet, I hear the words of my preceptor, who is protecting me from falsehood. (He weeps. Alas, father! Alas, venerable one! Alas, preceptor! Alas, lord! Alas, refuge of the world! Alas, ocean of compassion! Alas, bestower of fearlessness! Alas, protector of those who seek refuge! Alas, dispeller of the fears of the distressed! Alas, foremost of the twice-born! Alas, knower of the Vedas! Alas, knower of the self! Alas, knower of all beings! Alas, knower of the truth! Alas, knower of dharma! Alas, knower of the supreme goal! Alas, knower of the essence of the scriptures! Alas, knower of the meaning of the sacred texts! Alas, knower of the purport of the Upanishads! Alas, knower of the essence of the Purāṇas! Alas, knower of the essence of the Āgamas! Alas, knower of the essence of the Śāstras! Alas, knower of the essence of the Smṛtis! Alas, knower of the essence of the Itihāsas! Alas, knower of the essence of the Mantras! Alas, knower of the essence of the Tantras! Alas, knower of the essence of the Kalpas! Alas, knower of the essence of the Yoga! Alas, knower of the essence of the Sāṃkhya! Alas, knower of the essence of the Nyāya! Alas, knower of the essence of the Vaiśeṣika! Alas, knower of the essence of the Mīmāṃsā! Alas, knower of the essence of the Vedānta! Alas, knower of the essence of all knowledge! Alas, knower of the essence of all things! Alas, knower of the essence of all beings! Alas, knower of the essence of all worlds! Alas, knower of the essence of all times! Alas, knower of the essence of all states! Alas, knower of the essence of all actions! Alas, knower of the essence of all fruits! Alas, knower of the essence of all causes! Alas, knower of the essence of all effects! Alas, knower of the essence of all means! Alas, knower of the essence of all ends! Alas, knower of the essence of all paths! Alas, knower of the essence of all goals! Alas, knower of the essence of all dharmas! Alas, knower of the essence of all truths! Alas, knower of the essence of all mysteries! Alas, knower of the essence of all secrets! Alas, knower of the essence of all mantras! Alas, knower of the essence of all tantras! Alas, knower of the essence of all kalpas! Alas, knower of the essence of all yogas! Alas, knower of the essence of all sāṃkhyas! Alas, knower of the essence of all nyāyas! Alas, knower of the essence of all vaiśeṣikas! Alas, knower of the essence of all mīmāṃsās! Alas, knower of the essence of all vedāntas! Alas, knower of the essence of all śāstras! Alas, knower of the essence of all smṛtis! Alas, knower of the essence of all itihāsas! Alas, knower of the essence of all mantras! Alas, knower of the essence of all tantras! Alas, knower of the essence of all kalpas! Alas, knower of the essence of all yogas! Alas, knower of the essence of all sāṃkhyas! Alas, knower of the essence of all nyāyas! Alas, knower of the essence of all vaiśeṣikas! Alas, kn
"How is it that this superhuman voice does not grant me permission to enter the fray?
Alas! Oh, how painful!
Even the gods have taken the side of the Pāṇḍavas!"
In every way, Bhīma has drunk the blood of Duḥśāsana!
Alas, what misery, what misery!
Even while the blood of Duḥśāsana was being drunk, you remained indifferent!
What other favor can I do for Duryodhana in battle? (3.49)
"O maternal uncle, under the influence of Rādheya’s anger, we have acted ignobly;
therefore, you too should remain by the side of this king for now. Kṛpa said:
"I shall go there to provide a remedy;
you, however, should proceed directly to the encampment.
Having walked around [the stage], they both exit.
Thus ends the third act.
The fourth act begins:
Then enters the charioteer, carrying away Duryodhana, who is seated in his chariot and unconscious from a blow.
The charioteer walks about in agitation. [Offstage:

O you who have kindled a great desire for battle through the arrogance of your physical strength, and who have staked your entire store of life-force as a wager out of partiality for the Kaurava side!

Let the kings hold their ground! Let them hold their ground! The enemy forces are fleeing from the battlefield, their weapons slipping from their hands out of fear upon seeing Vṛkodara, whose appearance is loathsome as he is drenched in the blood remaining after he has drunk that of the slain Duḥśāsana.
Charioteer: [He continues.]

*Looking around:* How is it that he has arrived with his golden water-pot kissed by white, flickering fly-whisks, his banner indicated by the *vaijayantī* tied to its peak, and garlanded with a network of tiny bells producing a clamor from the uneven jolting caused by the crushing of thousands of the carcasses of slain elephants, horses, and men?

Having checked the expansion of the enemy's strength and prowess with a rain of arrows from his chariot, Kṛpa follows the King of Aṅga, who was attacked by Kirīṭin, while encouraging his own fleeing troops;
alas, a support has been born for our forces!

*From behind the scenes, after a tumultuous clamor:* "O, O warriors of the Kaurava army, and you soldiers who side with the Pāṇḍavas—your bows, swords, lances, and spears having slipped from your hands out of fear at the sight of me—do not fear! Do not fear!
Here I am, intoxicated by drinking the blood-nectar from the broad chest of the slain Duḥśāsana, moving with impetuous speed, with only a small portion remaining of the great festival of my vow!"

I call all of you as witnesses: Bhīmasena, the middle Pārtha, who was defeated at dice and enslaved by the Kaurava king—listen! Before King Duryodhana, whose wealth is honor and who bears the bow, in the presence of the Kuru kinsman and while Karṇa and Śalya look on, I have today drunk the warm blood from the chest of that man who dragged the hair and garments of the Pāṇḍavas’ wives, even as he lived, crushed by my sharp claws. (4.1)
Sūta:
(Hearing this, with fear) Ah!
The son of the Wind-god, that wicked-souled one who is like a gale uprooting the great forest of the Kuru princes, is indeed very near.
And let the Great King remain here for now,
unconscious; I shall drive the chariot very far away.
"Perhaps this ignoble man will act ignobly toward him as Duḥśāsana did toward him.
*Moving very quickly, looking around, and then:* "Ah! Here is that banyan tree, its thick foliage fanned by the cool, fragrant breeze scented by the stirring of the lotuses in the lake."
This place is a fitting site for rest for heroic men exhausted by the labors of battle.

Standing here, Your Majesty shall find your fatigue dispelled by this breeze from the lake—a breeze cooled by sprays of yellow sandalwood, naturally fragrant, suited to the change of season, and requiring no fanned palm-leaf fan.
Furthermore, with its banner lowered, this chariot will enter the shade without obstruction.
Having thus enacted the entrance:
"Ho there! Who is here?
(looking all around).
"Why is there no attendant here?
Surely, out of fear upon seeing Vṛkodara of such a kind and a master of such a sort, they have entered the camp itself.
Alas! Oh, what misery!"

Having granted Pārtha an assurance of safety, Droṇa did not protect the King of Sindhu; and while cruel deeds were done by this Duḥśāsana like unto a deer, Bhīmasena accomplished a feat in battle as if it were easy, fulfilling his vow against enemies that was otherwise difficult to achieve. Yet, I do not consider destiny—which has now turned its face away from the Kuru clan—to have attained its purpose even by this much.
(Looking at the king) Why does the Great King still not regain consciousness? Oh, how tragic! (Sighing)

Just as a forest, when its young trees have all been destroyed and only a single great śāla tree remains, is being ravaged by rutting female elephants, so too has this family—its princes all slain—been cast upon by the sidelong glances of Fate. // 4.3 //
Alas, O cursed Fate, you who are hostile to the Bharata lineage!
Even this vow of Bhīmasena—that he would slay the wielder of the mace while he is unhurt and unmounted—is being fulfilled by you. (4.4)
Duryodhana:
(Gradually regaining consciousness) Ah!
Does that wretched, evil-minded Vṛkodara have the power to fulfill his vow while Duryodhana is still alive?
Child Duḥśāsana, do not fear, do not fear!
Here I am, arrived.
O charioteer, surely drive the chariot to that very place where my child Duḥśāsana is.
Sūta:
Long-lived one, your horses are currently unable to pull the chariot,
nor even to fulfill your desire.
Duryodhana:
[Descending from his chariot, with pride and a hint of reproach] Enough of this delay in setting out on the chariot!
Sūta: (With embarrassment and compassion) May the long-lived one forgive me; may he forgive me!
Duryodhana:
Shame on you, charioteer! What is the use of a chariot?
For I, Duryodhana, am indeed one who moves solely for the purpose of clashing with and crushing the enemy.
"Therefore, with my mace as my sole companion, I shall descend to the field of battle.
Charioteer: "Long-lived one, it is even so."
"What doubt could there be?
Duryodhana said:
"If this is so, why do you speak thus? Look!"
"Before my very eyes, that wicked man, with weapon raised, intends evil against me, a fool naturally prone to mischief;
why do you not restrain me as I am so intent? Surely you have neither anger, nor compassion, nor even shame. (4.5)
The Charioteer:
(Falling at his feet with compassion) I make this request: *Please accept my humble submission.*
"O venerable one, that evil-souled wretch Vṛkodara must now turn back with his vow fulfilled;
it is for this reason that I speak thus."—
Duryodhana.
Suddenly falling to the ground:

"Alas, my child Duḥśāsana! Alas, you who have opposed the Pāṇḍavas despite my command! Alas, you whose sole delight was valor! Alas, you who were spoiled on my lap! Alas, lion among the herds of elephants that are the enemy clans! Alas, crown prince, where are you?
Give me an answer!"
Having sighed thus, he fell into a swoon.
The charioteer said:
"O King, take heart, take heart!"

Duryodhana: (Regaining consciousness and sighing) Even though you were cherished by me and by my elder brother, you have not been truly indulged in the pleasures of enjoyment as you desired; indeed, you have not been pampered in vain.
But for you, my child, I am the cause of this calamity, since I caused you to act with such immodesty and did not protect you.
[Thus he falls.
The Charioteer:
Long-lived one, take heart, take heart!
Duryodhana: Shame on you, charioteer! What have you done? You have acted toward a child who was always to be protected and who followed your commands.
I was protected by my brother Duḥśāsana as an offering.
Sūta:

O Great King, because the consciousness of the great chariot-warriors was carried away by showers of arrows, *tomaras*, spears, and darts that pierce the vital organs, the Great King was rendered motionless; thus, I have driven away the chariot.
Duryodhana:
O charioteer, you have done a great disservice;
for I was not awakened by the fragments of the thunderbolt-like mace struck against that very enemy of my younger brother, that beast of a Pāṇḍava,
nor did I quickly lie down upon that very bed of blood, drenched with gore, as either Duḥśāsana or Vṛkodara did.
*Sighing and looking toward the sky:* "O cursed Fate,
devoid of compassion and averse to the Bharata lineage! Could it be that death itself has come, yet Vṛkodara is not the slayer?"
The charioteer said:
"May evil be averted! May evil be averted!
Great King, what is this?"
Duryodhana: For me, whose kinsmen have been slaughtered without exception, what is the use of sovereignty or victory?
Then enters Sundaraka, his body adorned with bandages bound over wounds from arrow-strikes.
Sundaraka:
Noble sirs, have you perhaps seen the great king Duryodhana’s charioteer and second-in-command in this vicinity? (Looking around.)
Why does no one speak?
Very well;
a crowd of men with their attendants is seen here.
I shall go there and ask.

(Walking about and looking) Why indeed are these men, with their heron-feathered arrows whose tips cannot be pierced even by the mass of their thick armor, extracting the shafts from the hearts of their master who has been struck by a severe blow?
They certainly do not know this.
Very well;
I shall search elsewhere.
(Looking ahead and walking a little) Here indeed are these many heroic men gathered together; so, having gone there, I shall ask. (Approaching)
"Hey! Do you know in which direction the Kuru king is?
[Looking]—why are even these two weeping even more upon seeing me?
Therefore, surely they do not know either."
Alas! How truly most piteous is what occurs here!
This Vīramātā, having heard that her son has been slain by Śamala, follows him in death along with her daughter-in-law, who is dressed in red silk and adorned with all her ornaments.
(With praise) Excellent, Vīramātā! Excellent!
In another birth as well, may you have an unslain son.
Very well;
I shall search elsewhere.
(Looking elsewhere) Ah!
There, that host of warriors, their horses struck down by many blows and receiving no medical treatment, are lamenting while gazing upon this empty seat and this Tulaṅgama horse.
Surely their lord has been struck down right here.
But these do not know it at all.
Very well;
I shall go elsewhere and ask.
(Looking all around) Where is everyone? The people are distressed by the reversal of their fortunes, experiencing grief appropriate to their respective conditions. So whom shall I ask here?
Whom shall I blame?
Let it be;
I will search for it here myself.
(Walking about) Let it be. Now I shall reproach Fate.
Ho there, Fate! You who are the lord of eleven akṣauhiṇīs, the eldest brother of a hundred brothers, the husband of Gaṅgā, and the leader of Doṇa, Aṅgarāja, Śalya, Kṛtavarman, Sthāman, and the rest—*
Even the great King Duryodhana, the sole lord of the entire circle of the earth and the sun of the royal wheel, is being sought;
though he is being sought, it is not known in which region he resides.
*(Reflecting and sighing)*
Or rather, why should I blame fate here?

For this is the ripening fruit of that tree of gambling— the poison of the Jāṭu house— which has its sprouts in the words of Viśvāmitra’s harsh rebukes, whose roots have grown deep from the plucking of birds, which has been nourished by the neglect of his grandfather’s instructions, which has long been entwined with the enmity born of the seizing of Draupadī’s hair, and which has the seizure of the Pāñcālī’s hair as its flower.
(Looking elsewhere) Ah!

Here is seen a chariot with its shafts shorn, which, with its front facing the ten directions filled by thousands of divine bows produced from the rays of the sun augmented by the luster of various jewels, must surely belong to the great King Duryodhana for the purpose of his rest.
"I shall go and see.
[Having approached, seen him, and sighed:
"How is it that the Great King Duryodhana, being the lord of eleven Akṣauhiṇīs, sits here like a common man on this despicable ground, unworthy of his status?"
Or rather, this is indeed the ripening fruit of that seizure of the Pāñcālī’s hair.
Noble sirs, have you perhaps seen the great king Duryodhana accompanied by his charioteer in this region, or not?
Why does no one say anything?
Let it be;
here is seen a group of men with their girdles fastened.
I shall go there and ask.

How indeed do these [birds] extract the arrows from the heart of their own master, who has been struck by a severe blow, using their *kaṅka*-beaks which are difficult to pierce through the network of his thick armor?
Truly, they do not know this.
Very well.
"I shall search elsewhere.
Indeed, these other many heroic men are seen gathered here;
therefore, having gone there, I will ask."
"O, do you know in which direction the lord of the Kurus is?
Why is it that even these people, upon seeing me, weep even more intensely?
Surely they too do not know."
Alas! How truly most piteous is what is happening here!

This mother of a hero, having heard that her little son has been slain in battle, is about to follow him in death along with her daughter-in-law, who is dressed in crimson silk and adorned with all her ornaments.
Well done, O mother of a hero! Well done!
"In another birth as well, you will have your son killed. Very well;
I shall search elsewhere."
This other group of warriors, their bodies struck by many blows yet with their wounds still unbandaged, approaches this empty-seated horse and weeps.
Surely their master was slain right here;
thus, they truly do not know.
Very well;
I shall go elsewhere and ask:
"How is it that all these people, experiencing misfortune in accordance with their circumstances, are so distressed by their lack of fortune?"
So whom shall I question here,
or whom shall I reproach?
Let it be.
I shall investigate this myself.
Very well;
now I shall reproach fate.

"O Fate! Even the great King Duryodhana—who is the lord of eleven akṣauhiṇīs, the eldest of a hundred brothers, the protector of the circle of kings headed by Bhīṣma (the son of Gaṅgā), Droṇa, the King of Aṅga, Śalya, Kṛpa, Kṛtavarman, and Aśvatthāman, and the sole sovereign of the entire circle of the earth—is being sought.
Though he is being sought, it is not known in which region he remains."
Or rather, why should I blame fate in this matter?

For this [calamity] has indeed grown from the seed of the words of Vidura which were treated with contempt, from the sprout of the grandfather’s beneficial advice which was disregarded, and from the roots that took firm hold through the encouragement of Śakuni and others.

The fruit of that tree of poison which was the lacquer house and the gambling match—its basin having long been filled by the enmity rooted therein—is now ripening; its flower was the seizing of Draupadī’s hair.

Just as we see here this chariot, its flagstaff severed, filling the faces of the ten directions with thousands of rainbows produced by sunbeams mingled with the luster of various jewels, I conclude that this must certainly belong to the great king Duryodhana.
"I must go to the place of rest;
let me first investigate.
How is it that Duryodhana, the great king and leader of eleven akṣauhiṇīs, remains lying upon this despicable ground like an ordinary man?"
Or rather, this fruit of that seizing of the Pāñcālī’s hair by the flower is now ripening. [Approaching, he asks the charioteer with a sign. The charioteer:
*Having seen him:* "Ah! How is it that Sundaraka has arrived from the battlefield?
*Sundaraka:*
Victory, victory to the Great King!
Duryodhana: Victory, victory to the Great King!
*Looking around* Ah,
it is Sundaraka! Sundaraka, is all well with the King of Aṅga?
Sundaraka:
Your Majesty,
all is well with me in respect to my body alone.
Duryodhana:
(With agitation) Sundaraka,
has Kiritin slain his draft-oxen, killed his charioteer, or broken his chariot?
Sundaraka:
Your Majesty, neither has the chariot been broken,
nor even my heart's desire.
"Your Majesty, the chariot has not been broken,
nor even his desire.
Duryodhana said:
*With anger:* Why do you agitate my already distressed heart with these indistinct words?
Therefore, let it be told clearly and in its entirety.
Sundaraka:
As the Lord commands.
By the power of the crest-jewel of the Lord, the pain from my battle wounds has been removed.
*Thus, having walked about with pride:* "Let Your Majesty hear:
there is now one who slays the breath of the prince."

Ah! By the power of the crest-jewel of Your Majesty, the pain from my wounds in battle has been removed."
"May Your Majesty listen:
there is now the slaughter of Prince Duḥśāsana.
Charioteer: [He speaks.]
Sundaraka, speak!
Fate has already spoken:
Duryodhana.
"Let it be told; we have heard it.

"May Your Majesty listen."

Today, His Majesty King Aṅgarāja, enraged by the murder of Prince Duḥśāsana, with his forehead made terrifying by the knitting of curved eyebrows and raining down a multitude of iron arrows whose joining and release were imperceptible, has assailed that wicked man, the middle Pāṇḍava, who was already slain by Bhīmasena.
May Your Majesty listen!

Today, that wicked Bhīmasena—the wretch of the middle Pāṇḍava—has been assailed by our lord, the King of Aṅga, who is incensed by the slaughter of Kumāra Duḥśāsana; he, whose broad forehead is made terrifying by the knitting of his curved eyebrows, rains down a multitude of arrows whose fixing upon the string and their release are imperceptible.
Both: [listen].
And then what happened?
Sundaraka:

Then, O King, blinded by the spreading darkness created by the mass of dust raised by the horses, elephants, and foot-soldiers as they gathered with great force, and by the thick cloud of smoke arising from the multitude of overturned cooking-pots...
"By the force of our own army!
Indeed, the expanse of the sky cannot be discerned.

Then, O King, both armies were blinded by a vast darkness produced by the masses of dust raised by the glittering elephants, horses, and foot soldiers of both forces meeting together, and by the thick clouds of smoke from the collisions of the herds of elephants.
Indeed, the surface of the sky is not visible.
Both:
And then what? What happened next?
Sundaraka: Then,
O King,
by the deep and terrifying twang of the bowstring drawn back to its full extent, it was known that the clouds of the dissolution were thundering.
Duryodhana:
And then?
Sundaraka:

Then, O King, a storm of battle arose between those two, heralded by their mutual lion-like roars and thunder, radiant with flashes of blazing lightning falling from armor struck by various discharged weapons, featuring bows drawn deep like clouds, and raining down thousands of streams of arrows.
A stormy day of battle has arisen, with the bow as a cloud emitting deep thunder and raining down thousands of spreading showers of arrows.
Duryodhana:
What happened next? What followed?
Sundaraka:

And then, O King, in the meantime, Dhananjaya—fearing the defeat of his elder brother—mounted a great monkey stationed at the tip of his standard, which was emitting a harsh roar like a thunderclap; he appeared formidable with his four mighty arms bearing the marks of the conch, discus, sword, and mace, which were visible due to the dust raised by the galloping of his horses.
The sound of the chariot, filling the hollows of the ten directions with the deep resonance of its fivefold bells and the loud rattling of its excellent horses, rushed toward that place.

And then, O King, in the meantime, Dhananjaya—fearing the defeat of his elder brother—mounted a chariot whose great monkey atop the flagstaff let out a roar as harsh as the crash of a thunderbolt; it was difficult to behold, with its four long arms of Vāsudeva occupied in driving the horses and marked by the conch, discus, sword, and mace.
The excellent chariot, its ten directions and the hollows of the quarters filled with the echoing resonance of the loudly blaring *pāñcajanya* and *devadatta* conchs, rushed toward that spot.
Duryodhana:
And then? And then?
Sundaraka:
Then, seeing his father assailed by Bhīmasena and Dhanañjaya, he cast off his agitation and shook off his royal turban;
drawing his stiff bowstring back to his ear with his right hand, he raised an arrow whose nock was already struck by the friction of the string, causing his charioteer to cry out in haste.
Prince Viśasena arrived at that place.

Then, seeing his father attacked by Bhīmasena and Dhanañjaya, he cast off his turban in agitation, drew his hard bow back to his ear with the string, and, with the feathered end of an arrow raised in his right hand, hurriedly signaled to his charioteer.
Prince Vṛṣasena arrived at the region;
Duryodhana [spoke] with haughtiness.
And then what happened?
Sundaraka:
And then, O King, as soon as Prince Viśasena arrived, he shattered [the enemy] with arrows whose shafts were as dark and smooth as polished iron.
With its shafts dark-hued like hard iron, resembling hemp-fiber, and bound with smooth black stone and *sāla* wood,
Dhananjaya’s chariot was, in an instant, covered by those *śilīmukha* arrows as if it were a tree in full bloom.
And then, O King, even as he was approaching, that chariot was struck by Prince Vṛṣasena with arrows whose smooth, glossy feathers were as dark as polished sword-blades.
In an instant, Dhananjaya’s excellent chariot was covered by black-feathered, stone-sharpened, dark-tipped arrows, as if a tree were in full bloom with its shafts like bees. Both:
[With joy] "And then? And then?
Sundaraka:

Then, O King, Dhananjaya, raining down a shower of sharp, scattered, and fixed broad-headed arrows, said with a slight smile: "Hey there, Viśvasena! Even for your father, it would not have been proper to stand before me while I am enraged;
how much less so for you, a mere child?"
"Go then,
and fight with the other princes!
Having heard these words, [he was] made terrifying by the knitting of his eyebrows, which spread across his face as it became crimson with rage, kindled by the reproach of his elders.
The wielder of the *gaṇḍīva* bow was rebuked by Prince Viśasena with arrows that were piercing, harsh, uneven, and aimed well, but not with wicked words.
Then, O King, Dhananjaya, raining down a shower of sharp, well-aimed, and whetted *bhallā* arrows, said with a slight smile:
O Vṛṣasena, even for your father it would not be proper to stand before me while I am enraged; how much less so for you, a mere child? Therefore, depart!
"Fight with the other princes!

Having heard these words, he was reviled by Prince Vṛṣasena, who held a bow and whose face was reddened by a fury ignited by the insult from his elders; the prince’s countenance was made terrifying by the knitting of his eyebrows, and his harsh, uneven words—which pierced the vital spots—were cast upon him as they entered the path of his ears.
The wielder of the Gāṇḍīva [struck] with arrows, not again with wicked words.
Duryodhana said:
"Excellent, Vṛṣasena! Excellent!"
Sundaraka: And then what happened?
Sundaraka:

Then, O King, by Kirīṭin (Arjuna), who was filled with wrath born from the pain of the wound inflicted by the stroke of [Bhīṣma’s] arrow, and whose roar surpassed the thundering of the thunderbolt, having been conquered by the sound of his fierce *gaṇḍīva* bow...
"Then, O King, by Arjuna—whose fury was aroused by the pain of being struck by sharp arrows; whose roar from the string of his fierce *gāṇḍīva* bow surpassed the sound of a thunderbolt;
and who blocked the range of vision with the falling of his shafts—a certain marvel was performed that was worthy of his training and strength."
Duryodhana:
(With a hint of irony) And then? And then?

Sundaraka: And then, O King, having seen that [display], Prince Viśasena— his hand rendered restless by the drawing, aiming, and releasing of arrows, and by the swift movement of his bowstring, quiver, and bow—
executed the same martial feats with even greater distinction, disregarding the enemy’s proficiency in obstructing the battle.

Then, O King, having observed such skill of the enemy in the maneuvers of battle— his unhesitating drawing of the bowstring from the mouth of the quiver, his swift movement of hand as he took up, aimed,
and released arrows— Prince Vṛṣasena also engaged in the work of war with particular distinction.
Duryodhana:
And so it went.
Sundaraka:

Then, O King, at this juncture, having ceased from the affliction of battle and momentarily relaxed their pursuit of enmity, both the armies of the Kuru king and the Pāṇḍavas cried out, "Well done, Prince Viśasena! Well done!"

Then, O King, at that moment, the host of heroes—having ceased their engagement in battle and rested for a short while from the pursuit of enmity—began to raise a clamor, exclaiming, "Bravo, Prince Vṛṣasena!
Bravo! regarding both the armies of the Kuru king and the Pāṇḍavas.
Duryodhana began to look around,
filled with wonder.
And then what happened?
Sundaraka:
And then, O King, although Sūda was possessed of prowess that surpassed the entire circle of archers, nevertheless—

While the Lord Aṅgarāja was caught in a dilemma by joy, anger, and compassion due to the simultaneous occurrence of equal deeds, a shower of arrows fell upon Bhīmasena, while his gaze, clouded with tears, fell upon Prince Viśasena.
And then, O King, [the sight] of his son, who possessed prowess that surpassed the entire circle of archers, in such a state...

At the commencement of the battle, as his lord, the King of Aṅga, stood in the perilous straits of joy, rage, and compassion, a volley of arrows fell upon Bhīmasena, while his gaze, clouded with tears, fell upon Prince Vṛṣasena.
Duryodhana:
[It is] full of danger here and there.
Sundaraka: [What is it?]
Then, O King, by the wielder of the *gaṇḍīva* bow— who was enraged by the heroic deeds performed by the force of our army and who blazed with a rain of arrows—
a shower of shafts was simultaneously unleashed against the horses, the charioteer, the excellent chariot, the bow, the bowstring,
the Nala-bannered standard, and even the moon-disc.
Then, O King, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow— incensed by the shouts of "Bravo! arising from both armies and raining down a shower of arrows—
discharged a simultaneous torrent of shafts against the horses, the charioteer, the excellent chariot, the bow, the string, the royal insignia, and even the white parasol.
Duryodhana: (With fear) And then?
And then?
Sundaraka: Then,
O King, the prince—
deprived of his chariot and with his bowstring severed— proceeded to move in circular maneuvers, having merely prevented the flight of arrows by the act of whirling around.
Duryodhana: (With apprehension) And then?
And then?
Sundaraka:
Then, O King, incited by the wrath of his own defeat, the lord Aṅgarāja, disregarding the battle with Bhīmasena, loosed a shower of arrows upon Dhanañjaya.
The prince also, having mounted another chariot brought by his attendants, again began to engage in combat with Dhanañjaya.
Then, O King, the Aṅga king, his wrath inflamed by the destruction of his excellent chariot and disregarding the assault of Bhīmasena, released a shower of arrows upon Dhanañjaya;
the prince, having mounted another chariot brought by his attendants, likewise set out once more to fight with Dhanañjaya.
Both: [The two of them...]
"Excellent, Vṛṣasena, excellent! And what happened next? Sundaraka replied:
Then, O King, the prince said:

"Ho there, you loud-mouthed one who insults your father, O Madhyama-Pāṇḍava! My arrows do not fall upon anything other than having left your body. Having said this, he covered the Pāṇḍava's body with thousands of arrows and began to roar with a lion's roar.
Having spoken thus, he covered the body of the Pāṇḍava with thousands of arrows and began to roar with a lion's cry.
Duryodhana [said] with astonishment:
"Oh, what prowess this child possesses, despite his innocent nature!
And so it goes...
Sundaraka:
Then, O King, having shaken off that shower of arrows, Arjuna—filled with wrath born from the impact of those fixed shafts—seized the *śakti* from the seat of his chariot;

it resounded with the tinkling of a network of golden bells, was as pure as the sky freed from the obstruction of clouds, possessed a face dark and glossy like a sapphire, and was both terrifying and beautiful to behold, radiant with the luster of various jewels. He seized it with a laugh.
Then,
O King, having warded off that shower of arrows, Arjuna— his wrath aroused by the impact of those sharp shafts—

seized her from the seat of the chariot; she was facing the prince, and as she was released, she resounded with the tinkling of a network of golden bells, like the stainless vault of heaven freed from the obstruction of clouds.
The spear, with its sharp, dark, and glossy tip, its appearance both terrifying and beautiful, radiant with the luster of various jewels,
was hurled with a mocking laugh toward Kumāra by Duryodhana.
[With dejection] Alas! And then? And then?

Then, O King, upon seeing the flaming spear, the bow with its arrow slipped from Aṅgarāja’s hand, the heroism dear to warriors departed from his heart, tears flowed from his eyes, and a cry broke forth from his mouth. Then, O King,
the spear,

having been gazed upon for a long time by Prince Vṛṣasena with sharp, razor-headed arrows drawn back to his ear, was split into three pieces midway, like the Bhāgīrathī by the Blessed One, the Three-Eyed Lord.
Śakti:
Duryodhana:
Well done, Vṛṣasena! Well done!
And then what happened?
Sundaraka:
And then, O King, in the meantime, the sound of the battle drums was drowned out by the clamor of the world of heroes shouting cries of "Bravo! in a tumultuous uproar.
Then, O King, in that interval, the sound of the battle drums was drowned out by the shouts of "Bravo! from the assembly of heroes, which resounded with clamor;
and the field of battle was covered by a shower of flowers released by the hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
Duryodhana:
Oh, what prowess this child possesses! What happened next? What happened after that?
Sundaraka:
And then, O King, it was said by my lord, the King of Aṅga:
"O Viśvadalla, your task and mine are not yet finished."
Therefore, grant me a moment;
let us first behold the proficiency in the science of archery of both your dear son and your brother.
This spectacle is worthy of being seen by you as well.
Then, O King, the lord Aṅgarāja said:
"O Vṛkodara, my engagement in battle with you is not yet finished;
therefore, grant me a moment."
"Let us first observe the proficiency in the science of archery of your dear son and your brother;
this must also be observed by you," said Duryodhana.
And then what happened?
Sundaraka:
Then, O King, having ceased their violent engagement in battle for a moment, both Bhīmasena and King Aṅga became pacified in their enmity and looked upon one another.
SktCh_128: Then, O King, when they ceased their persistent engagement in the conflict, both Bhīmasena and the King of Aṅga became spectators for a moment, their hostilities pacified.

And then?

And then, O King, in the meantime, Gaṇḍīvin, enraged by the breaking of his bow, said:
"Are you [the ones] headed by Duryodhana?
Having said this much, he mimes bashfulness.
Then, O King, in the meantime, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, provoked by the breaking of his shafts, spoke:
[The King said: "Are they here, headed by Duryodhana?
Duryodhana:
"Sundaraka, let it be told."
This is the speech of another:
Sundaraka:
May Your Majesty listen.

O Duryodhana and the other leaders of the Kuru army! O you who steer me toward immodesty, O Karṇa! While I was out of sight, you surrounded these two sons of mine with many great serpents and tormented them.
But now, even as you all look on, I shall reduce this prince Viśasena to nothing but a memory.
Having said this, he proudly brandished the Gāṇḍīva bow, which was terrifying with its life-force roar resembling the thundering crash of a lightning bolt;
the Lord also readied the Kālapuṣṭa.
Let Your Majesty listen!

O you who are the leaders of the Kuru forces headed by Duryodhana! O Karṇa, whose helmsman is lack of discipline! While I was out of sight, my dear son Abhimanyu was surrounded and slain by many of you great chariot-warriors.
But now, even as you look on, I shall leave this young bull of the Vṛṣṇis as nothing more than a memory.
Having spoken thus, he proudly struck his *gāṇḍīva* bow, which produced a life-shrieking sound as terrifying as the crash of a thunderbolt;
the Lord also readied his *kālapṛṣṭha* bow.
Duryodhana:
(With feigned indifference) And then?
Sundaraka:

Then, O King, when the commencement of the battle-work by Bhīmasena was forbidden, two rivers of arrows were created by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, which swept away the banks consisting of the chariots of Vṛṣasena and Ratha-kūlaṅkaṣa, the kings of Aṅga. By those two [rivers], whose excellence of training was displayed through their mutual affection, that difficult-to-approach central island was overwhelmed.
Furthermore, that ill-behaved middle son of Pāṇḍu, Duryodhana, was diligently instructed by those two others, who displayed exceptional training born of mutual affection.
[Duryodhana:
"And then? What happened next?"
Sundaraka:

*Looking up*—Ah!
It is the Blessed One, the Lotus-Eyed One, and my dear son Kirīṭin.
Blessed One, I offer my salutations.
"To the Diademed One:** Come, come, my child!
Arjuna bows down."
Yudhiṣṭhira said to Vāsudeva:
"O Lord, what victory could there be for him other than victory itself, for whom the Blessed One, the ancient Puruṣa Nārāyaṇa himself, pronounces blessings?"

Having contemplated You—who have assumed a form born from the great agitation of the *guṇas* such as *mahat* and the rest; who are the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*); who are the cause of the arising, destruction, and abiding of all beings; who are unborn, immortal, and inconceivable—not even one who merely contemplates You in this world becomes miserable, O Lord, let alone one who beholds You.
*Embracing Arjuna:* "My child, embrace me.
Kṛṣṇa:
O Great King Yudhiṣṭhira,
this venerable Vyāsa, these sages such as Vālmīki and Rāma, and the army commanders headed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna led by the sons of Mādrī,
have arrived together with the Magadhas, Matsyas, and Yādavas who are obedient to your command, carrying jars of water from sacred fords upon their shoulders for your royal consecration.
"But I, having perceived that you were being harassed by the evil-minded Cārvāka, have come here with Arjuna with the utmost speed.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"How have we been thus deceived by the Rākṣasa Cārvāka?"
Bhīmasena:
(With anger) Where is that friend of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, that outcaste among the Puṇyajanas, by whom such a great derangement of the noble one's mind was caused?
Kṛṣṇa:
That wicked-souled one has been captured by Nakula.
Therefore, tell me, O Great King, what further desired object shall I accomplish for you?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O lotus-eyed one, when the Blessed One is pleased, there is nothing that he does not give;
yet I am content with a mind that is common to ordinary men."
Indeed, I am not able to request anything further than this;
let Your Majesty behold:

the entire host of enemies has been destroyed by those blinded by wrath, yet we five remain unhurt; and the ocean of humiliation produced by my own misconduct toward the princess of Pañcāla has been crossed.
O God, Supreme Person, you speak to me, a doer of good deeds, with such regard; what else could I possibly ask of you, the Blessed One, other than this, now that you are so well-pleased?
Nevertheless, if the Blessed One is even more pleased, let this be so:
may people live out their full span of life, free from wretchedness, disease, and fatigue; O Blessed One, may there be devotion to the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) without duality;
and may the king—beloved by the world, a kinsman to the learned, a discerning knower of virtues, and ever virtuous—remain with his realm well-governed.
Moreover:
May the protectors of the earth guard the earth; may the row of clouds bestow rain upon the world; may the ground be filled with grain.
O Muranarakāra, may my devotion to you arise through the yoga of non-duality for a very long time, and may the gods consume the sacrificial oblation.
Kṛṣṇa: So be it. [Thus they all exit.]
Thus ends the sixth act.
This concludes the drama named *Veṇīsaṃhāra*.
And this lamentation was uttered by that poet, whose mind was distressed by the separation from a clever and affectionate [beloved].
Those royal swans, who were addicted to poetic discourse and elegant sayings, have departed;

those assemblies have come to an end; and the speech of the virtuous, which was once praiseworthy even for its smallest fragments of merit, as well as the voices of poets—so clear, sweet, and full of aesthetic flavor and ornamentation—are now gone.
May this great work, which has escaped destruction, flourish throughout the circle of the earth.
